title: Driving Through the Gaps: How the Minibus Taxi Industry Rewrites Spatial Planning from Below
content: In many cities of the Global South, the minibus taxi industry operates as the backbone of informal or semi-formal public transport, yet its relationship with statutory spatial planning remains critically under-examined. This paper investigates how the minibus taxi sector shapes and is shaped by land-use regulation, urban form, and mobility infrastructure. Drawing on a case study of a major South African metropolitan area, the research employs a mixed-methods approach combining spatial analysis, policy review, and semi-structured interviews with taxi operators, municipal planners, and commuters. Findings reveal a persistent spatial mismatch between taxi route networks, formal land use zoning, and transport interchanges, leading to congestion, unsafe boarding points, and limited integration with land development. Furthermore, the study identifies how exclusionary planning practices historically marginalised the taxi industry, resulting in informal adaptation strategies that now complicate regulatory reform. The paper argues for a relational spatial planning framework that recognises the taxi industry as a legitimate land use and mobility actor. Policy implications include rethinking transit-oriented development, upgrading taxi ranks as multi-functional public spaces, and co-producing planning regulations with industry stakeholders. This research contributes to debates on transport-land use integration in contexts of informality and rapid urbanisation.
